title: England cricket curfew: Only wins for Joe Root's side will stop hokey-cokey
description: "We are grown men and we know how to behave," said Joe Root."As an international cricketer you are always representing the badge. We are a group of ad
body: "We are grown men and we know how to behave," said Joe Root."As an international cricketer you are always representing the badge. We are a group of adults and we feel we can be treated like that."Root did not say these words in 2026, but in his first stint as England captain in 2017.It was the eve of an Ashes tour, one on which Root was without Ben Stokes because of the incident outside a Bristol nightclub.The trip to Australia included the Jonny Bairstow-Cameron Bancroft 'headbutt' and Ben Duckett tipping a drink over James Anderson. The low point was Moeen Ali, a practising Muslim, being asked by a local journalist if he and the rest of the England players would be able to "stay out of the pub".The midnight curfew imposed on that tour lasted more than four years until it was banished in 2022.What is it about an away Ashes that drives Englishmen to drink? Trouble on the latest trip resulted in the return of the curfew in January yet, seven months later, Root's comeback as captain has seen the curfew, erm, put to bed.Goodness knows what it says about the state of the England men's team that the subject of 'when grown men should go to bed' has been live for almost a decade.You can be forgiven for struggling to keep up with England's hokey-cokey over the curfew in the past few months.As a quick recap, rules that were introduced to the white-ball team in January were kept in place for the Test side at the beginning of the home summer.After the first Test, captain Stokes and Gus Atkinson broke the curfew. Director of cricket Rob Key, fed up after a winter of misdemeanours, floated the idea of a total alcohol ban, while also admitting Atkinson didn't know the curfew was in place.Head coach Brendon McCullum conceded there was some "ambiguity" around the regulations at the same time Stokes and Atkinson were cleared of any wrongdoing. Stokes came back, then retired.Last month, England issued new guidelines to players, with the curfew still in place and advice for alcohol not to be drunk on the days immediately before, during, or immediately after a match.Then McCullum was sacked as Test coach. His last act in charge of both the Test and white-ball teams was to relax the drinking guidelines so England's T20 side could celebrate their series win against India.Now the curfew is gone, under the instruction of Root and McCullum's replacement as Test coach - his great mate Stephen Fleming.The England and Wales Cricket Board see Fleming as a grown-up, and he has made a grown-up move, one that also includes the curfew being lifted from a white-ball team still led by McCullum and Harry Brook.McCullum is said to be supportive of players taking responsibility for their behaviour, which begs the question as to why he went along with the curfew in the first place.Perhaps this is not a problem specific to this group of England players. Last week, Stokes rejected the idea that England have a drinking culture, instead suggesting the whole game has an unhealthy relationship with alcohol.And that is not to say it is a crime every time a beer touches the lips of a cricketer.In 2022, when England stunned New Zealand at Trent Bridge to give birth to the Bazball movement, the players celebrated on the dressing room balcony with a few drinks, then kicked on into the early hours and the Mega Munch takeaway in Nottingham.After the Ashes of 2005, probably England's greatest series win, celebrations were led by a swaying Andrew Flintoff on an open-top bus through the streets of London.Even this past winter, there's a decent chance Travis Head put away more than the England players. It's just that Head was scoring runs and Australia were winning.Former cricketers will argue that any drinking taking place now is nothing worse than what was consumed in years gone by - Ian Botham, Allan Lamb, Phil Tufnell and the rest.But perhaps that's exactly the point. Cricket has not moved with the times. You wouldn't catch famous Arsenal swillers Paul Merson and Tony Adams saying Declan Rice and Viktor Gyokeres could match them drink for drink.It is also not fair to pin a drinking culture only on elite players. Cricket has a relationship with alcohol right down to the grassroots of the game.I play league cricket (badly), mainly as an excuse to have a few beers. On a Saturday, I couldn't really ask my partner to look after our two children just so I can go to the pub with 10 of my mates. Instead, I have to keep up the pretence of trying to score runs and catching the ball as a wicketkeeper. The cricket is a hindrance to getting to the bar.Not that cricket will be too different to other amateur sports - back to the pub after Sunday league football, meeting in the bar at the tennis club, drinking games after a rugby match.Has cricket kept up with the professional versions of those sports? Very much open to debate.But these wider problems of the entire game are not an excuse for an England team who, frankly, would be given a pass for endless hours after midnight if they were winning.Trouble is, they aren't, with only two victories in their past 10 Tests. The reputational damage that has been suffered over the past year will only be fixed by success on the field.The first opportunity to start putting things right comes with three matches against Pakistan, beginning next week. After that, England's Test future is about as tough as it gets, with the major series coming away to world champions South Africa this winter, a home Ashes against Australia next summer, then five Tests in India in early 2028.Does lifting the curfew enhance their chance of winning those series? Maybe treating the players like grown-ups off the field helps on it."If you want guys to take responsibility on the field, they've got to feel like they can be grown adults off it and make good, strong decisions off it," said Root on Wednesday.Either way, England must decide their stance and stick to it. Much like constantly changing an opening pair does little for the team's output of runs, flip-flopping on rules around behaviour does not create a winning environment.Curfew or no curfew, England can only rebuild on the field, not in the bar.Win Tests, series and trophies, then they can go to bed as late as they please.

schema.headline: England cricket curfew: Only wins for Joe Root's side will stop hokey-cokey

title: Trump says Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt to leave post
description: Leavitt has had a sometimes combative relationship with the media during her tenure, accusing some reporters of being biased or left-wing.In February
body: Leavitt has had a sometimes combative relationship with the media during her tenure, accusing some reporters of being biased or left-wing.In February last year, her office seized control of the White House press pool, stripping organisational duties from the White House Correspondent's Association, as well as initially barring the Associated Press over its refusal to adopt the term "Gulf of America".Among supporters of the Trump administration, however, she was widely praised for remaining "on message" and ferociously defending the president's policies."Watching it in person was even better than watching it online," Fox host and conservative activist Riley Gaines wrote on X after one particularly feisty briefing room exchange. "Karoline Leavitt is so good at her job."She is the second longest-serving press secretary in either of Trump's administrations, following only Sarah Huckabee Sanders.It is unclear who will now become Trump's sixth chief spokesperson across his two administrations.During Leavitt's roughly seven-week maternity leave earlier this year, a series of senior Trump administration figures took the podium including Vice-President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Secretary of the Interior Doug Bergum.The BBC has contacted the White House for comment on potential choices and the timeline of her replacement's selection.In an interview with Fox News on Wednesday, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller - who called Leavitt a "close friend" and "role model"."We're going to continue working together every single day," he added. "Her story is just beginning. I can't wait to see what her future holds."

schema.headline: Trump says Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt to leave post

title: Results, appeals and resits - what to do if your A-levels don't go to plan
description: Image source, PA MediaUpdated 27 minutes agoHundreds of thousands of A-level students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland have opened their results
body: Image source, PA MediaUpdated 27 minutes agoHundreds of thousands of A-level students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland have opened their results.They were released at 08:00 BST on Thursday 13 August.Those who have applied to university should be able to see whether they have been successful too, as the Ucas Hub updates at the same time.Here is everything you need to know about results, appeals and resits.What are the 2026 A-level grade boundaries?Each exam is graded on a scale from A* to E.Grade boundaries show the minimum number of marks you need for each grade.They are decided by assessment specialists at each exam board every year and are only published on results day.Some exam boards, like AQA, external, have their old grade boundaries for previous years' exams published on their website.How can I appeal against A-level results?If you do not think your grade is right, you should first talk to your school or college.It will contact the exam board on your behalf and ask for your marks to be reviewed.If you still think you have been unfairly graded after a review, you can ask your school or college to appeal., externalThe exam board will consider whether a correction is needed.If you are still not satisfied, you can request a review from the exams regulator Ofqual.It's a similar story if you are unhappy with your T-level or BTec grades - you will need to speak to your school or college first as students cannot appeal directly to the exam board.What if I don't get the A-level grades I hoped for?If you only just miss out on the grades you need to get on to a university or college course, the admissions office might accept you anyway or offer you a place on a different course. You could also try applying for a different place through the clearing process - see more details below.It may also be possible to resit some or all of your exams. Talk to your school or college if you want to explore this route. Exam resits for A-levels will take place in May or June 2027.What is Ucas university clearing?The Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (Ucas) runs a clearing process matching students with university and college courses which still have spaces., externalStudents can use it if they:Fail to achieve the grades for their conditional offerFail to receive any offers they want to acceptDecide after 30 June to apply for universityAchieve better grades than expected and want to change universitiesClearing opened on 2 July and closes on 19 October.Universities make an offer to a student to join a course based on qualifications and grades or the Ucas tariff points system., externalEach A-level grade is worth a certain number of Ucas points. For example, an A* is worth 56 points and a D is worth 24 points.Many students decide not to go to university and start an apprenticeship or go straight into work.Others take a gap year, external so they have more time to decide what to do next.When is results day in Scotland?

schema.headline: Results, appeals and resits - what to do if your A-levels don't go to plan

title: Major Russian grain export terminals hit in Ukraine Black Sea port attack
description: A "massive" Ukrainian drone and missile strike on Russia's port of Novorossiysk has damaged two major grain export terminals and hit the last big Russ
body: A "massive" Ukrainian drone and missile strike on Russia's port of Novorossiysk has damaged two major grain export terminals and hit the last big Russian naval base on the Black Sea, reports say.Three people, including an eight-year-old child, were killed and another 24 injured in the overnight attack, local officials said.Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv had launched rockets, jet and naval drones in a "unique operation" to strike the Russian base, although he did not mention grain terminals being hit.Ukraine's military later said four Russian warships, including two frigates, were hit. Russia has not commented on the issue."The occupying fleet and all the infrastructure that supports it will not be safe as long as Russian aggression continues," Zelensky said in a post on social media. Most of Russia's Black Sea fleet is docked in Novorossiysk - one of the largest ports in Russia - after it was forced to vacate its former home base of Sevastopol, in the Russia-occupied Crimean peninsula, which was too exposed to Ukrainian attacks.The attack follows an uptick in the exchange of strikes in the Black Sea this summer, after a period of relative calm.A major grain trading company confirmed to Russia's TASS news agency that its terminal had been hit in the attack on Wednesday, while another told Reuters and Russian outlet RBK the same.The Russian agriculture ministry announced on Wednesday that it was working to redirect cargo flows to ports in the Baltic and Caspian Seas as well as land routes. It did not make any reference to Ukraine's attacks but said it was "taking into account current logistical constraints".Repeated explosions reportedly rang out over Novorossiysk throughout the night as air defences shot down aerial objects. An emergency situation was declared in the city on Wednesday, after the barrage of drones struck areas around the port and damaged pipelines, suspending water supply for the city. Elsewhere in the region a man was killed by drone debris, regional Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said. Several locations in the surrounding Krasnodar region were also struck by "several hundred drones" overnight, Kondratyev added, with dozens of buildings damaged, including homes. For its part, Moscow launched aerial overnight strikes which killed at least 11 civilians in Ukraine between Tuesday and Wednesday. The majority were killed when Russia hit the southern city of Zaporizhzhia with ballistic missiles and glide bombs.In an interview with CNN, Zelensky said that Ukraine would need a tenth of the current US stockpile of interceptor missiles to stop all Russian ballistic missile attacks. Five percent of the stockpile would get Ukraine through winter, he added. He said this year Ukraine has two and a half times fewer interceptors than it did in 2025, while "Russia has two times more ballistic missiles per month than they had before."Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The last remaining sea route out of Ukraine has been badly affected by several deadly Russian strikes on cargo ships and the port of Odesa, through which Moscow seeks to put off foreign companies from trading with Ukraine. In July, the Ukrainian Agribusiness Club (UCAB) reported a 23% decrease in exports.Meanwhile, Ukraine has grown increasingly adept at carrying out long-range strikes on Russian territory. Its recent attacks on vessels in the eastern Black Sea have disrupted Russia's grain shipments, too.Russia is the world's largest wheat exporter - but according to a Moscow-based analytics company, exports for August could fall by more than half compared to the same month over the last five years due to the disruption in the Black and Azov seas.On Wednesday, Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accused Ukraine of carrying out strikes on Russian grain and agricultural infrastructure, resulting in a hike in global food prices and growing grain shortages.But Zakharova also said that Russia would continue striking "facilities that [Ukraine's armed forces] use on the Black Sea to destabilise the navigation situation" until "the full elimination of threats to security projected to the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea".Concerns over how the war in Ukraine would affect global food supplies have been persistent since the start of Russia's invasion in 2022.Together, Russia and Ukraine account for a significant share of global grain trade, particularly for buyers in North Africa, the Middle East and parts of Asia.The 2022 Black Sea Grain Initiative, under which Russia agreed to lift its blockade on Ukraine's agricultural exports, did not last after Moscow resumed attacks on vessels using the maritime corridors to Odesa the following year.

schema.headline: Major Russian grain export terminals hit in Ukraine Black Sea port attack

title: European Athletics Championships 2026: Matthew Hudson-Smith wins historic 400m gold
description: On his childhood track, in front of a stand named in his honour, hometown hero Matthew Hudson-Smith was not going to be denied.A full-circle moment, c
body: On his childhood track, in front of a stand named in his honour, hometown hero Matthew Hudson-Smith was not going to be denied.A full-circle moment, completed by writing his name in history. More than two decades after stepping foot inside Alexander Stadium for the first time aged nine, Hudson-Smith delivered Great Britain's latest gold in Birmingham to become the joint-most decorated man of all-time at European Championships.The 31-year-old celebrated the third European 400m title of his illustrious career by making his way into the crowd and placing a hand on the banner bearing his name.Moments before, Hudson-Smith had stormed down the home straight, just as he had countless times before as a member of local club Birchfield Harriers.This time, though, the Olympic and world silver medallist did so to rapturous cheers inside the arena which fostered his love for the sport.With his eighth podium at the championships, Hudson-Smith equalled French sprinter Christophe Lemaitre's men's record medal tally - with the relays still to come."Honestly, words can't describe how much that meant to me," he told BBC Sport."Nobody was going to beat me on this track. This is my home. I know this track like the back of my hand. I have my stand. Now I'm going to go for Mayor of Birmingham and Wolverhampton!"I knew I was the best in the world. I knew that, on paper, I was a second faster than every single one of these guys. It was about me and the clock."Born in Wolverhampton, Hudson-Smith said before the championships that it would "mean the world" to land gold not only on home soil, but where he first began working towards his dreams.With his achievements since those early training sessions recognised in writing on the north stand, to Hudson-Smith's mind there could be only one possible outcome.He did not make it easy for himself, however.Entering the championships as the fastest European this year, the Briton admitted he "misjudged" his semi-final after fading to second place in his heat - an error which meant he had to pursue gold from the outside lane.Unable to monitor the early progress of his rivals, Hudson-Smith went out hard and had established enough of a gap entering the home straight to reassure the home fans that all was under control.The European record holder over 400m, and the sixth-fastest man of all time in the one-lap event, missed out on successive global titles by mere fractions of a second at both the World Championships in 2023 and Paris 2024 Olympics.Those stunning silvers followed the toughest period of his life, but he put three years of "absolute hell" behind him to win world bronze in 2022 as he re-established himself among the world's best.On the European stage, there has been no shortage of golden moments - but none will come close to this emotional full-circle moment.Gold was secured in 44.17 seconds, with Frenchman Muhammad Abdallah Kounta next to cross the line in 44.40.Speaking on BBC TV, three-time world heptathlon champion Dame Jessica Ennis-Hill said: "What a moment. This will stay with Matthew Hudson-Smith forever."It means so much and the pressure was piled on him. Anything but a gold medal here for him would have been a disappointment."

schema.headline: European Athletics Championships 2026: Matthew Hudson-Smith wins historic 400m gold

title: Aston Villa: Striker Brian Madjo makes impressive entrance after eight months in limbo
description: Villa had fought since the start of the year to register the 6ft 4in Madjo following his £10m arrival from Metz.Under-18 players cannot complete inter
body: Villa had fought since the start of the year to register the 6ft 4in Madjo following his £10m arrival from Metz.Under-18 players cannot complete international transfers, but the club argued that since Madjo was born in London he should be exempt - despite having three caps for Luxembourg in friendlies. Since those games, he accepted an England Under-17 call up last year and has four goals in nine appearances, scoring on his debut against Venezuela. With England searching for their next No.9 once Harry Kane eventually retires, Madjo could force himself into the conversation in the coming years.Fifa does allow some exemptions for minor players to make moves, including if a 16 or 17-year-old transfers within the European Union - something the UK is no longer part of.The battle was finally won just eight days ago - after Villa took their case to CAS in July - and Madjo was added to the travelling party for Salzburg, having not been included in the initial squad.With Ollie Watkins rested after World Cup duty and Tammy Abraham left on the bench, the youngster was given the responsibility up front by Emery having scored four pre-season goals. His strike at the Red Bull Arena, holding off Ecuador international Willian Pacho to volley in John McGinn's cross, was arguably the hardest chance of the trio he had in a first half full of promise. It cancelled out Khvicha Kvaratskhelia's opener for PSG, only for Desire Doue to hit a second-half winner after a video assistant referee (VAR)  check.Before his goal, the hulking Madjo had earlier planted a free header over from three yards and shot wide, but was a constant nuisance for 11-time Ligue 1 winner and Brazilian centre-back and captain Marquinhos. "He played because he was showing us his capacity to work and be demanding," said boss Emery. "It is not just about scoring goals, it's about defending and how he has the commitment and discipline tactically. He was doing that. "I wanted to play with young players and watch their progression. Brian started scoring goals [in pre-season] against Walsall and Real Sociedad."Now the reality is we have shown their capacity, but they have to keep being consistent, demanding and keep performing at the level they were."Villa have been looking to sign a new striker - Chelsea's Nicolas Jackson has been a summer target - but Madjo's availability now gives Emery a different option and dilemma before the Premier League season opener at Brighton on 23 August."You've got a young player coming, especially on a stage like this one, against PSG, getting in those scoring positions and not allowing that disappointment to stay with you," former Villa striker Dion Dublin told BBC Radio 5 Live."I saw Brian Madjo, he had his hands on his head for a couple of seconds and then he got into another scoring position."He was brave enough to get back into that scoring position and if he keeps missing it's not frightening him. He's happy to have that pressure on his shoulders. I've been there, you need to be able to deal with it. At 17, he seems to be doing it easily."Madjo - and fellow teenage forward George Hemmings - were given their chance against PSG with Emery insisting he would not rush Watkins, Emi Martinez and Ezri Konsa back for the game.The trio are due to return next week after being given a month off following the World Cup, with Martinez losing the final with Argentina and Watkins and Konsa helping England to third place. Madjo expertly deputised for Watkins, despite missing his earlier first-half chances, until he was replaced by Abraham with 18 minutes left.Whether Konsa will still be a Villa player for the league opener against Brighton remains open to debate with Arsenal expected to step up their pursuit of the defender.Villa have already sold Morgan Rogers in a record £117m deal to Chelsea and Youri Tielemans to Manchester United, and Konsa's departure would be a another bitter blow after winning the Europa League last season and qualifying for the Champions League.Keeper Martinez will stay, despite interest from Juventus this summer. Emery added: "We decided to play this match with the players who were ready to play, were fit and trying to avoid some risk with some players. It is very important how we are going to manage the players."I am trying to use my experience to avoid some mistakes which i can understand can happen."I can feel free with my decision and proud of the players."

schema.headline: Aston Villa: Striker Brian Madjo makes impressive entrance after eight months in limbo

title: Leading doctor rebukes NHS chiefs over transplant crisis
description: Image caption, Professor Derek Manas is frustrated by the "last-minute" cancellation of transplant operationsByMichael Buchanan Social affairs corresp
body: Image caption, Professor Derek Manas is frustrated by the "last-minute" cancellation of transplant operationsByMichael Buchanan Social affairs correspondent and Adam EleyA senior doctor has blamed NHS chiefs for numerous problems within transplant services in England and called for an overhaul in a leaked letter seen by the BBC.Professor Derek Manas, the medical director of NHS Blood and Transplant, admonished NHS England for creating a system with a burnt-out workforce, "few consequences for poor performance" and operations cancelled "last-minute".The number of heart and lung transplants the NHS carries out each year has not increased in 30 years.NHS England, the national management body for the health service in England, said it was "working hard to improve these life-saving services".'Unpredictable' utilising of organsWhile NHS Blood and Transplant manages organ donations and supports transplant centres, services are commissioned and paid for by NHS England.But in a letter to NHS England and a small group of patient advocates, Manas said the central body had created a "fragmented" system "with poor accountability".There is a "mismatch", he said, between each hospital's waiting lists, organ availability, capacity to carry out surgeries and the availability of operating theatres.This is "leading to last-minute cancellations [and] unpredictable utilisation of donated organs," he warned.The BBC reported in March that the UK, once a world leader, had fallen behind major Western nations in heart and lung transplantation, though it fares better in other areas such as kidney transplantation.The NHS transplants one in 10 lungs and one in seven hearts that are donated - half the proportions seen in some other countries.It has not invested in modern technology at the same rate as other countries, and suffers from a lack of theatre space, intensive care beds and staff.Wales and Northern Ireland do not have a heart and lung transplant centre, so patients commonly travel to England for surgery. There is one heart transplant centre in Scotland.Image source, BBC NewsImage caption, Some hospitals have far shorter waiting lists than othersWaiting times for donated hearts can vary greatly - from eight months to four-and-a-half years - depending on the hospital.Manas said NHS England had "never actively managed" waiting lists, and "seldom" tried to make it fairer.In addition, half of the six UK heart and lung transplantation centres have lost their top surgeon in the past two years, as the medics seek opportunities abroad.Manas said "inadequate" workforce planning had led to "burnout among transplant surgeons and teams, recruitment and retention difficulties [and] increasing reliance on goodwill. We have a system that assumes the consultant workforce will absorb pressure indefinitely."Issues in the heart and lung transplantation service were first outlined in 2024 in a report by international experts, commissioned by the Conservative government.NHS England, which was tasked with implementing report recommendations, said it had worked to "improve outcomes for patients", but surgeons and campaigners believe progress has been slow.Image source, PAImage caption, Former health minister Dr Zubir Ahmed says the NHS must avoid operations being cancelledAmong those who believe the system should change is Dr Zubir Ahmed, who was the health minister responsible for transplantation until he quit Sir Keir Starmer's government in May.The Glasgow MP and kidney transplant surgeon told the BBC some elements of the transplant system were "world leading", such as being free at the point of care.But he called for NHS Blood and Transplant to be granted the power to commission services across the UK as part of ministers' planned closure of NHS England, so that patients could be moved swiftly to get the organ they need."I don't think there is ever a need to cancel a transplant because of capacity issues," Ahmed said.In a statement, NHS England said transplant services are "complex and impacted by many factors, including the number of organs made available for transplantation, but the NHS is working hard to improve these lifesaving services"."NHS England is leading a programme of work which is already helping to increase the number of transplants, reduce variation, identify suitable patients earlier and improve access," it added.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: Leading doctor rebukes NHS chiefs over transplant crisis

title: Newbridge fire affects five homes in Caerphilly county
description: Newbridge councillor Gary Johnston told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast on Thursday that the county council would support people affected by the fire "in an
body: Newbridge councillor Gary Johnston told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast on Thursday that the county council would support people affected by the fire "in any way we can"."The council will be looking at what we can do for them, to get these families somewhere to stay," he said. First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth thanked emergency services and told Radio Cymru Dros Frecwast his sympathies were with "everyone affected", and "especially those who have had to leave their homes because of this fire."Newbridge RFC said the club is "absolutely heartbroken" in a post on social media. The club has offered to supply hot and cold drinks, and provide showers and changing facilities to "anyone who needs it".South Wales Fire and Rescue Service received a call-out on Wednesday at 16:00 BST.The Welsh Ambulance Service also sent a specialist team and two ambulances."Members of the public are urged to stay away from the area to allow emergency services to operate safely," said the fire service.

schema.headline: Newbridge fire affects five homes in Caerphilly county

title: How do I apply for an apprenticeship and what will I get paid?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByEducation correspondentUpdated 20 minutes agoApprenticeships offer a route into work and further qualifications for people
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByEducation correspondentUpdated 20 minutes agoApprenticeships offer a route into work and further qualifications for people who want to learn while earning.But what is an apprenticeship, how much do apprentices get paid and what careers can they lead to?What is an apprenticeship and what job could I get?An apprenticeship combines paid work with study towards a recognised qualification.Apprentices usually spend most of their time working and part of their time completing training with an employer, college, university or online provider.People often choose apprenticeships because they know the career they want to pursue, or because they want to gain new skills without studying full-time.Any employer can hire apprentices. They are responsible for ensuring apprentices work with experienced staff and receive time away from their job to complete their studying.Apprenticeships are available across a wide range of industries, including business, engineering, construction, healthcare, digital, hospitality and creative sectors.How much are apprentices paid?You get paid for the time you spend working.If you are under 19, or if you are 19 or older but in the first year of your apprenticeship, you will be paid at least the apprentice rate, external of £8 per hour. Those over 19 - or who have already completed their first year - are entitled to the appropriate minimum wage for their age:£10.85 for 19 and 20-year-olds£12.71 for those aged 21 or aboveThese rates apply across the UK but employers can choose to pay more than the legal minimum.Some apprenticeships can also lead to higher salaries after completion.What are the different levels of apprenticeship?In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, the different levels of apprenticeship are:Intermediate (Level 2 - GCSE standard)Advanced (Level 3 - A-level standard)Higher (Levels 4, 5, 6 and 7 - foundation degree or above)Degree (Levels 6 and 7 - bachelor's or master's degree)In Scotland, the different levels are:Foundation (mostly SCQF Level 6 - Highers standard)Modern (mostly SCQF Levels 6 and 7 - Highers or Advanced Highers standard)Graduate (SCQF Levels 9, 10 and 11 - undergraduate or master's degree standard)Advanced apprenticeships - A-level standard - are the most popular, and the number of people doing higher apprenticeships has been rising.How many people do apprenticeships and what could change?Hundreds of thousands of people are on apprenticeships in England each year.Apprenticeships are available for school leavers, young people and adults looking to develop new skills or change careers.The government has introduced a number of measures aimed at increasing apprenticeship opportunities and helping more young people access training.There have also been concerns about the decline in the number of young people starting apprenticeships in recent years, as well as whether opportunities are equally accessible to people from different backgrounds.How do you find an apprenticeship?If you know where you want to work, you can head straight to the employer's website and apply.You can search for apprenticeship opportunities through different official websites in England, external, Scotland, external, Wales, external or Northern Ireland, external. The Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (Ucas) website, external also lets you search for apprenticeship vacancies. You will be interviewed for the apprenticeship before you start, and will need to pass an assessment showing what you have learned before you can finish.Think hard about what the apprenticeship offers. Can you picture yourself in a job in the industry? Will the qualification help you in the career? What opportunities exist at the organisation itself?Make sure you understand what training you will receive, how much you will get paid, and how long the placement will last. You can also read reviews of apprenticeships on sites such as RateMyApprenticeship.co.uk., externalWhat are some of the problems with apprenticeships?Some apprentices do not complete their training.Reasons for leaving early can include personal circumstances, changing career plans, problems with the quality of training or not receiving enough time to study.Ucas has previously warned that young people were being put off by a range of barriers, including:low paylack of availabilityhaving to apply for apprenticeships individuallyThe government has introduced changes to apprenticeship rules in England, including reforms to course requirements, as it tries to increase the number of opportunities available.

schema.headline: How do I apply for an apprenticeship and what will I get paid?

title: ICE equipping agents with gloves that deliver electric shocks
description: Unlike a taser, which uses sharp barbs in the skin to deliver a shock of up to 50,000 volts, the gloves do not complete an electrical circuit inside t
body: Unlike a taser, which uses sharp barbs in the skin to deliver a shock of up to 50,000 volts, the gloves do not complete an electrical circuit inside the body.The gloves instead deliver a sharp shock to convince a subject to comply using "pain deterrence", says Lt Butch Gallion, an administrator at Hawkins County jail in Tennessee."We may or may not deploy them. It just depends on how they act. When you push the button to turn them on there's a light that displays. The inmates understand that light, and often just seeing the light brings compliance," he says.The shocks can only be delivered when they contact skin, allowing an officer to touch a subject's clothing, and then move to the skin – typically the wrist or elbow - if they begin to fight.If they become combative, he continues, "then you can apply the gloves to an area that the skin is exposed. And it's an instant complier for me".According to the DHS note, GLOVE would be used by officers and agents in Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), which targets transnational criminal organisations, and Enforcement Removal Operations (ERO), which is responsible for arresting, detaining and deporting people who violate immigration laws in the US. Some law enforcement agencies are already using the gloves but it's believed that the planned ICE purchase would be the largest from Compliant Technologies to date.  Civil rights groups, including the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), have expressed alarm about law enforcement using them. "ICE spent the last year showing this country that they are willing to disregard the law and are too quick to use force, with devastating and at times fatal consequences for citizens and noncitizens alike," said Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy director on policing at the ACLU.  Federal immigration agents have been criticised in the wake of fatalities that have occurred during enforcement operations.Recent incidents include the fatal shooting of Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas, while Colombian national Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero was killed during an immigration enforcement operation in Maine.ICE has also been under pressure to deliver President Donald Trump's deportation agenda, which includes meeting a daily target of arrests."Now they [ICE] might be equipped with a device that allows them to deliver an electric shock with their hands by pushing a small button, in a move that might be imperceptible to those watching," Borchetta said. "Giving immigration agents a concealed means of delivering terrible pain is a recipe for more harm to the public and less accountability."With reporting by Max Matza

schema.headline: ICE equipping agents with gloves that deliver electric shocks

title: Newspaper headlines: 'The sun, the moon' and 'The greatest show on Earth'
description: Dramatic images of the eclipse feature on almost all of the front pages. The Daily Telegraph calls, external it "the greatest show on Earth". "Once in
body: Dramatic images of the eclipse feature on almost all of the front pages. The Daily Telegraph calls, external it "the greatest show on Earth". "Once in a generation" is the headline in the i Paper, external while, for the Daily Express, external, it was "heavenly wonder".  The Daily Mail says, external Britain finally got a break from the Sun, if only for a few minutes.The front page of the Sun, external shows simply the paper's name in its traditional masthead, style then the thin crescent of light visible during the eclipse, then the words "The Moon". The paper says John Lewis reported a 40% spike in colander sales, as people were able to use them to safely observe the sun's progress. "Unlike eclipse glasses," a spokesperson for the store said, "you can use it to strain your spaghetti for dinner afterwards". The Daily Mirror says, external hundreds of observers gathered in Greenwich Park, and a reveller tells the paper "there were Champagne corks popping" at the peak of the eclipse.The Guardian leads, external on the warning from the Royal College of Nursing that its members are working in "inhumane" conditions, because of the high temperatures. Its general secretary Professor Nicola Ranger says this should be a "wake-up call" and the paper says Prime Minister Andy Burnham is being pressed to "fully acknowledge" the need to adapt to a changing climate.The Daily Telegraph reports, external that the prime minister's plans to house asylum seekers in wealthier parts of the country would cost more money than current arrangements. The government tells the paper it seeks to "fairly" house asylum seekers across the UK.The Times reports, external that the government's own analysis of its plans to restrict zero hours contracts suggests they will drive up costs for businesses by up to three-billion pounds a year.   The government has said it is consulting on the proposals and is committed to giving workers greater income security.The Financial Times reports, external on tensions in England and Scotland's rural communities where the grouse season began yesterday. Residents have reported deep concerns that the cultivation of heather, used as a plentiful food source to keep the population of birds high, is a health risk because of its flammability in dry conditions. "It's like we're sitting on a petrol station," one tells the paper.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'The sun, the moon' and 'The greatest show on Earth'

title: How to get a good night's sleep during hot weather
description: Image source, Getty ImagesUpdated 25 June 2026A period of extreme heat across the UK this week has broken records for the hottest day and night temper
body: Image source, Getty ImagesUpdated 25 June 2026A period of extreme heat across the UK this week has broken records for the hottest day and night temperatures ever recorded in June.It can be hard to sleep during periods of hot weather, but these simple tips could help. 1. Don't let yourself napHot weather can make you feel tired and lethargic during the day. That is because you are using more energy to regulate your internal temperature.But if your sleep is disturbed at night, try to avoid napping during the day. When it is hot, feeling sleepy can be precious - save it for bedtime.2. Keep to your normal routinesHot weather can encourage you to change your habits. Don't. That can disrupt your sleep patterns. Try to keep to your usual bedtime routine, and do the things you normally do before bed.3. Remember the basicsTake steps to make sure your bedroom is as cool as it can be at night.During the day, close the curtains or blinds to keep out the sun. Make sure you shut the windows on the sunny side of your home, to keep out hot air.Open all the windows before you go to bed, to get a through breeze.4. Use thin sheetsReduce your bedding but keep covers handy. Thin cotton sheets will absorb sweat. Wearing loose-fitting clothes made of natural fibres like cotton or linen can keep you cooler than sleeping naked. However hot it is in your bedroom, your body temperature will fall during the night. That is why you sometimes wake up feeling cold even though the temperature is higher than usual. 5. Use a fan and chill your socksUsing even a small fan can be sensible in hot weather, especially when it is humid.It encourages the evaporation of sweat and makes it easier for your body to regulate your internal temperature.If you don't have a fan, try filling a hot water bottle with ice cold liquid instead.Alternatively, cool socks in the fridge and put those on. Cooling your feet lowers the overall temperature of your skin and body.6. Stay hydratedYou should make sure you drink enough water throughout the day but should avoid drinking very large amounts before bed.Image source, Getty ImagesIt's about striking the right balance. You don't want to wake up thirsty - but you don't want to have to take an additional trip to the bathroom in the early hours either.7. But think about what you drinkBe careful about soft drinks. Many contain large amounts of caffeine, which stimulates the central nervous system and makes you feel more awake.Avoid drinking too much alcohol as well. Many people drink more when the weather is hot.Alcohol might help you fall asleep but it also promotes early morning waking and a poorer quality of sleep overall.8. Stay calm - and leave your phone aloneIf you are struggling to sleep, get up and do something calming. Try reading, writing, or even folding your washing.But avoid using your phone. Mindless scrolling might seem appealing, but the blue light from the screen can stimulate your brain and leave you feeling more awake. Return to bed when you feel sleepy.9. Keep to the usual bath and bed times for childrenChildren are often quite robust sleepers - but they can be very sensitive to changes in family "mood" and routine.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lukewarm baths can help before bedtime during hot weatherMake sure usual bedtimes and bath times do not go out of the window just because it is warm.As part of the bedtime routine, the NHS UK website, external recommends lukewarm baths. Make sure they are not too cold, as that will boost your child's circulation which could increase their temperature.A baby cannot let you know if they are too hot or too cold, so it is important to monitor their temperature. They generally sleep best when their bedroom temperature is between 16C and 20C - use a room thermometer to check. 10. Remember that you will be OKMost of us need about seven to eight hours of good-quality sleep each night to function properly.Teenagers, children and babies typically need more sleep because they are still growing.But remember that the majority of people can still function well after a night or two of disturbed sleep.Although you might yawn a little more frequently than usual, you will probably be fine.These tips were based on suggestions by Prof Kevin Morgan, former director of the Clinical Sleep Research Unit at Loughborough University, and Lisa Artis, of the Sleep Council. This article was first published in July 2019.

schema.headline: How to get a good night's sleep during hot weather

title: Fan tips: Experts advise how best to use yours during a heatwave
description: No air con? Here's how to get the most out of your electric fan ByEsme Stallardclimate and science reporter and George SandemanStruggling to work and
body: No air con? Here's how to get the most out of your electric fan ByEsme Stallardclimate and science reporter and George SandemanStruggling to work and sleep without air con? Your trusty electric fan could help more than you think - but only if you put it in the right place.During the recent heatwaves, social media was full of advice on how to make your fan work harder - but some of it was conflicting. So, to try to clear up any confusion, we asked experts to separate fact from fiction - from which part of your body to direct your electric fan at, to the best room in the house to put it. Keep windows open or closed? The first thing most people will want to know is if opening a window and using a fan at the same time will cool down their home.It depends, says Becci Taylor, a specialist in building physics at the engineering firm Arup.She says it's best to try to keep the air in your home as cool as possible, so you should keep the windows closed during the daytime, when temperatures outside are likely to be at their highest.She recommends drawing curtains and blinds in rooms facing direct sunlight to stop the air inside heating up. "If the air is cooler than your skin temperature, it's going to cool you down even without sweating," she says.You could place a fan in the coldest room and use that to direct its air towards the rest of your home. Though she advises only doing so if you have a reasonably large or powerful fan.If you have a small fan, then it doesn't particularly matter where in the room you place it on a hot day, says Taylor - provided you keep your windows shut. "You just want it to be near you."At night-time, when the air outside is likely cooler than the air in your home, you should consider opening a window and using a fan to bring in the cooler air.Placing the fan next to the open window and pointing it inwards, towards the rest of the room, can help.But pointing the fan towards the window - to try and blow the hot air in your home outwards, as some social media posts advise - isn't particularly useful as you would not get the cooling benefits of having it pointed towards you.Body or face? Where you should point itPointing the fan directly at your face may be tempting during periods of extreme heat, says Prof Mike Tipton from the University of Portsmouth. But he says that will only give you the perception of "thermal comfort" - in other words you will feel cooler but you're not actually cooling as much as you might think.A specialist in human and applied physiology, he says a fan should be directed more broadly at your body and, crucially, placed far enough away so it "provides air movement over the [whole] body".That air movement improves the effectiveness of your sweating, he says, which is caused by your body naturally trying to cool itself down.Using a fan this way works particularly well if you combine it with other methods of keeping your body temperature down, adds Prof Tipton, such as keeping your hands cool and taking tepid showers.However, if you have young children, you should not point a fan directly at them as it could cause dehydration. Instead, you can use the fan to circulate air around the room.Now for an icy blast Putting a bowl of water or ice in front of a fan will also help, Taylor says. That's because the air movement encourages water in the bowl to evaporate, which takes heat out of the air, making the room a little cooler.You can buy fans that come with a misting device, she adds. Taylor says smaller, handheld versions are most effective indoors.Too much mist increases humidity, which reduces your body's ability to sweat and cool down as there's more moisture in the air. Buying a version that is too large means "you just end up with a very sweaty, damp room", she says."Sweating and misting work in the same way, which is also why it's comfortable and cooler to be near a fountain or open body of water," she says."You can harness that mechanism by putting some liquid in front of the fan, which can evaporate."One important tip is never cover your fan with a wet or frozen towel to try and achieve the same effect, as some social media posts demonstrate, as it can cause electrical safety problems.The 35C debateYour body's temperature is about 37C, while your skin is likely to be about 34C.When the air temperature in your home is less than this a fan is helping you sweat, feel cooler and take away heat from the skin.As the air temperature moves above this, Taylor says a fan can still help to evaporate your sweat - as long as it is not too humid - but it will also bring more heat to your skin.The government advice is not to use a fan once it exceeds 35C inside.Met Office scientists have said there is an increasing likelihood of extreme temperatures in the UK, and that the chance of exceeding 40C is accelerating.Taylor adds: "If people can understand how the physiology of cooling works, then we can start to help them deal with the heat better."Illustrations by Jodi Lai.

schema.headline: Fan tips: Experts advise how best to use yours during a heatwave

title: The town making missiles for Trump
description: 'If you're not conservative, don't come here': The town making missiles for TrumpFigure caption, ‘Justified’ or 'no business being there’? Tennessee m
body: 'If you're not conservative, don't come here': The town making missiles for TrumpFigure caption, ‘Justified’ or 'no business being there’? Tennessee munitions town loyal to Trump but divided on IranBySheila FlynnSenior US Reporter, Kingsport, TennesseeAs one local puts it, there's a "church on every street" of the Appalachian community of Kingsport, in the US state of Tennessee.Christianity reigns supreme in this working-class area. Above downtown's historic Lamplight Theatre, a sign proclaims "Jesus first in all things".And while more than 300 area churches may be providing spiritual sustenance to this town of 58,000 people, there's another institution that supplies it with economic nourishment.The Holston Army Ammunition Plant churns out explosives used in Patriot missiles, warheads and other heavy weaponry in the midst of the country's costly and prolonged war with Iran.The war, and its knock-on effects on everything from gas to groceries, has led to a steep decline in President Donald Trump's approval ratings. Recent polling has placed his approval at an historic low of 32% - down 14% from when he first took office in January 2025 - with many Republican respondents citing disillusionment with the president's policies.Image source, Eloise AlannaImage caption, Veteran David Carter, 66, is an outspoken Christian who supports US action in IranThe two big drags on the president's popularity are the cost of living and the Iran War, with one bleeding into the other. The conflict has caused gas prices in the US to spike to above $4 a gallon, a painful hike to any US business that relies on transport.But in Kingsport, support for the president approaches an almost-religious fervor. The city voted overwhelmingly for Trump in all three of his elections. So did wider Tennessee, a Republican state for more than 25 years.When it comes to the Iran conflict, most residents either outright support the military action or rationalise the war's necessity - despite Trump's repeated campaign promise of "no more wars"."If he can stop anyone from having a nuclear bomb, then I'm for it," says Pam Robinson, 65, who spent 20 years working at the local chemical plant.David Carter, a bearded veteran who plays Santa Claus at Christmastime, says "the whole reason we go over there, and we keep everything under control there, is [so that] we don't have it on our doorstep."Others are more blunt."Honestly, I think we should turn them into a parking lot and don't worry about it anymore," says veteran James Camper, 63, wearing a Trump lanyard around his neck as he exits a discount grocery.Veterans account for around 10% of the region's population, and many other households have active duty family members.Robinson, a staunch Christian and independent voter who says her faith informs her candidate choices, believes the remote nature of the war may be preventing local people from being more upset with Trump."Let me say this: If it was hand-to-hand and more people were getting killed, people would be banging the doors down," she says.Image source, Eloise AlannaImage caption, Daniel Overstreet, 53, believes Trump's 'hands are tied' by CongressKingsport's position as a main munitions manufacturer - with Holston standing as the only domestic supplier of some essential explosive and propellant components -  gives its residents a unique perspective when it comes to the war in Iran.The plant employs around 1,000 people and is just one of many sprawling industrial complexes standing out starkly from the lush Appalachian Mountain landscape."The plant's going to be open regardless of whether we're at war or whether we're not," says Daniel Overstreet, 53, standing next to his Harley Davidson in downtown Kingsport. "It is what it is."He believes Trump and the administration are "doing a great job" but there are "too many people trying to fight him.""[He said] he would get the gas prices under control, and they were for a while," says Overstreet. "He said he was gonna get food prices down, but he has no control over that. The president is basically a puppet for Congress and the Senate."His hands are tied, to a certain extent."It's not that people here don't complain about high gas and food prices, inflation and other economic woes - it's just they don't blame Trump for any of it."He's done good on some things; I think he needs to check his advisers and see on some things," says Robinson. "I think he's advised wrong on some things."It was Trump himself, however, who announced his decision to strike Iran in February 2026 following failed negotiations. In an eight-minute video posted to social media, he said "the objective is to defend the American people by eliminating imminent threats from the Iranian regime" - and claimed Iran "will never have a nuclear weapon".Image source, Eloise AlannaImage caption, Evangelist William Bogle believes Trump is 'imperfect' but was the best 'alternative'Evangelist William Bogle, 75, voted for Trump every time he ran and believes the president is "doing a good job" - even though his wife "has to stretch a grocery dollar until, you know, it's big as a bedsheet".Trump is "just gonna have to do a little bit better in some things than he's doing right now," he says."I know he wants the country to prosper."This stalwart support reflects a deeper truth sometimes hidden in the polling headlines. Although Trump has lost favour among more traditional Republicans and independent voters, his base - who self-identify with his "Make America Great Again" mantra - remains much more steadfast in backing him.So while much of the US watches to see how much Trump's sliding popularity may damage Republicans in November's midterm elections, here in the Bible Belt, sometimes red is the only option.As voters turned out last week for local elections, the ballot included a single Democratic candidate. Of the county commission's 11 districts, seven featured only Republicans running, with some unopposed.Many say they can't and won't cross party lines for moral reasons, citing abortion as the single biggest deciding factor, with opposition to socialism and "woke" issues too hard for them to ignore.Those fears outweigh any personal criticisms they may have, says David Carter, 66, a grandfather and Christian as well as a veteran.Trump needs to humble himself more, he concedes, but Carter would only consider a candidate who "supports the morals" of the population. That means opposing  abortion, for example.Image source, Eloise AlannaImage caption, Democrat Adam Teague points out 'there's a church on every street' in KingsportThose who hold more liberal views exist in Kingsport, but they're vastly in the minority and less vocal.Piercing artist Adam Teague, 44, is a gay, heavily-tattooed Democrat working in downtown Kingsport."Before Trump took office, I was wearing, like, rainbow shirts and everything," says Teague, who was raised Baptist. "I kind of toned it down, just to feel safer."Trump was triumphant in the 2024 election in part because of his ability to attract a diverse coalition including people of all ages and races. But while his Maga supporters are sticking by him, polling suggests that many young people who helped get him over the line against Kamala Harris are now disillusioned.Mary Herron, 21, who is leaving a boutique cupcake shop with two friends, has noticed a difference in attitudes amongst her contemporaries."I am seeing a shift in the support … that's kind of rare around here," says Herron, a student who works part-time. "But I've seen a handful of people who have been like, 'Oh yeah, well, I voted for him, and now I'm not with him anymore'."Image source, Eloise AlannaImage caption, Caden Bayless, Mary Herron and Emily Villalpando are 21-year-old progressivesTrump first entered politics when the women were in middle school, says her friend Emily Villalpando, 21. "So a lot of the people that we grew up with kind of just adopted their parents' views."And so now that we're growing up, we're having more responsibilities," says Villalpando, who's studying biomedical science and wants to be a doctor. "The economy affects us a lot more."The three college students - their friend Caden Bayless makes up the trio - cite women's rights and heavy-handed immigration agents as major concerns, but they are sceptical of major attitude or voting shifts in the region. Bayless said she is hopeful the younger generation can make a change, but "given where we live … it would be a very difficult change."Bogle, summing up the Kingsport region, inadvertently speaks to their fears."We live in a great place, and if you're not conservative, don't come here," the preacher says. "Because you wouldn't be a good fit. But if you're conservative, come here, and we'll embrace you."He'll be praying for Trump, he says, as will the more moderate Robinson."All you can do is pray for your leaders, and God will give you what you want in the end," she says.

schema.headline: The town making missiles for Trump

title: How to get the most out of university clearing on results day
description: Clementine Wade, an education consultant and content creator, says there are things students can do to prepare for clearing. She suggests writing down
body: Clementine Wade, an education consultant and content creator, says there are things students can do to prepare for clearing. She suggests writing down all possible outcomes that you could get, and then finding alternatives to those outcomes. For example, depending on available places:If I get AAA, then I could do physics at SussexBBC could be physics at AberystwythCCD could be physics at Nottingham TrentIf you are doing BTecs, T-levels or other qualifications, you can work out how many Ucas points your results are worth using the calculator tool on their website, external.The Ucas website has a search tool to find courses, which you can find here, external. You can filter the options to the year of study, type of course and to those with clearing vacancies. It is the only official vacancy list, so it is the most up-to-date.For those who are unsure about their course choice and want to change, Wade says it is important to talk to a trusted adviser first, like a family member or teacher. She says students should think about why they chose that option in the first place, and why you might now be changing your mind.She says she finds most of the people who go through clearing are those that are applying to university for the first time.Haadi Nasir, a student at the University of Manchester, was one of those people. At first, he wanted to take a gap year after his A-levels so did not apply for university, but was persuaded to go by family and friends after achieving "great grades". On the day, with the help of his A-level teachers, he filled in a Ucas form, applied to six universities via clearing and picked the University of Manchester to study politics and modern history. "The good thing about clearing is that you can apply to as many universities as you want, unlike with Ucas, where you are limited to five," he says."That was definitely stress-relieving," he says.For those on the fence about university, Nasir recommends people put in a Ucas application "just in case" to avoid the stress of results day. That's a piece of advice that is echoed by Wade."You will need a referee, which is why I'd suggest doing it now," she says."Let's say [you've] got to email the teacher, the teacher's got to add a reference, then Ucas only gets sent once all of those parts are sent together."Nasir says he wished he was more prepared for clearing, and advises students to write down some notes on location, accommodation and cost for each university you contact. "Make sure you know whether you qualify before calling," he says."With my university I was required to have a specific A-level, so make sure you meet the requirements."For those awaiting results, Ucas updates at 08:00 on results day, so you can often find out whether you have been accepted to your firm choice before knowing your grades. But Wade advises holding off and waiting until you get your results before you open the Ucas website. "I would say try and steer away from the temptation, get your results in hand and then look at your Ucas track, because then you can action that decision as opposed to having 90 minutes of freak-out."Jamie Bradford, head of future students at Leicester De Montfort University, also says it is easier to start conversations about clearing with your results in hand. On Ucas, before you add a clearing choice in your application, you need to contact the university or college and give them your clearing number - which you can find in your application - and personal ID, so they can find it."It's amazing how many students don't actually talk about the course or the place at all," says Bradford. "All they want is just the offer - 'I've got these grades, can you take me?' - in reality, it's three or more years of your life. The university is a big decision."Bradford says students need to ask about the day-to-day of the course, the campus and whether accommodation is available. "Work up a priority list," he says."For us, it's about fitting the right student to the right course, not just about getting any offer."Wade says students should go through a list of alternatives, and once they have received offers and discussed student finance with the universities, have a break to chat with a trusted person. She also stresses that students need to have the confidence to pick up the phone and call universities. "I know it feels scary, but you are the client, you do get to ask these questions," she says."You don't even need to ring this university to say, 'Can I get into this course, please?' You could say, 'Hey, what course could you offer me?' Because you know what, universities need these students."Some universities, like Leicester De Montfort, also operate clearing through WhatsApp as well as via phone.

schema.headline: How to get the most out of university clearing on results day
